data.title: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest
data.excerpt: Brill has published István Zimonyi’s Muslim Sources on the Magyars in the Second Half of the 9th Century. For anyone interested in hillforts it matters because it describes the life and warfare of the Old Hungarians just before they entered the Carpathian Basin: nomads in felt tents, moving to the river banks before winter, raiding the Rus and the Slavs for captives to sell on to the Byzantines as slaves, and led by two rulers, one of whose titles they had taken over from the Khazars.

children.text: Some time ago Brill published István Zimonyi’s book Muslim Sources on the Magyars in the Second Half of the 9th Century. For a „hillfort person“ it is interesting because it describes the life and warfare of the Magyars just before their arrival in the Carpathian Basin. There is no point in commenting on the whole book, and so I deal only with the information that I consider important for understanding their successful „conquest of the homeland“ (honfoglalás).

Even though in the book the author uses the designation Maďar, Maďari – in English, of course, simply Magyars, without any qualifier – I am not convinced that today’s Hungarians are unreservedly the descendants of the Magyars described in the book, and that is why I write about the „Old Hungarians“.

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: Muslim historians use the designation Magyar in various written forms, for example Ibn Rusta in the form majghir or majghar. Sometimes the designation Bashkir also appears in the records as bāshjird, bāshqird, but whether the Bashkirs can always be understood as the „Old Hungarians“ is a highly specific problem and lies beyond the scope of this short article. By way of orientation only, these were probably people of the Muslim faith who came to the Carpathian Basin either with the „Old Hungarians“ or later, and settled in the south of Hungary with the permission of the Magyar princes, or of the first Hungarian kings. In any case, the Bashkirs were probably already neighbours of the „Old Hungarians“ in their original homeland in the steppes below the Urals.

The „Old Hungarians“ are described in the Muslim sources as a Turkic people. The Byzantines, too, called the Magyars Turks, and did so even at a time when the emperors were marrying the daughters or sisters of Hungarian kings who bore Slavic names. The Slavic name Uhri, which Western Europe took over, likewise originates in the designation Ungri, Ugri, by which the Slavs in the Carpathian Basin referred to the first Turkic people they encountered, that is the Onogurs, and which they then secondarily applied to the „Old Hungarians“ as well.

It follows unambiguously from the records that the „Old Hungarians“ led a nomadic way of life in the steppes north of the Black Sea. Indeed, the information about the Magyars obtained in 942 from a captured Magyar in Andalusia shows that in the Carpathian Basin too they lived as nomads in yurts at least until the middle of the 10th century.

blocks.text: They have neither towns nor houses, but live in felt tents scattered across the country.
blocks.author: Ibn Ḥayyān
blocks.source: quoted after I. Zimonyi: Muslim Sources on the Magyars in the Second Half of the 9th Century

children.text: Unlike nomads in warmer latitudes, the nomads of the Eurasian steppe have to supplement their sources of subsistence with plunder and hunting, because of the snow that makes grazing the herds difficult in winter.

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: Ibn Rusta writes that the „Old Hungarians“, who lived north of the Black Sea between two rivers, moved before winter to the banks of the rivers, where they supplemented their food supplies by fishing. Fishing was an important source of subsistence and other historians mention it in connection with nomadic communities in the European part of the steppe as well. In De administrando imperio its author, Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, writes in chapter 40 that the Magyars live by the rivers Temes, Tutis, Maroš, Kriš and Tisa. His record was made around 948 and likewise shows that the Old Hungarians were still living as nomads even fifty years after their arrival in the Carpathian Basin.

The question of whether the „Old Hungarians“ were at least partly farmers before their arrival in the Carpathian Basin is resolved in the book in a very odd way. Besides the Muslim records, which clearly write of a nomadic way of life, the archaeological finds from their original homeland also prove that the „Old Hungarians“ lived as nomads. Among the bones of livestock those of cattle and horses markedly predominate, and there are no bones of the domestic animals usually associated with farming. Even so, on the grounds that the „Old Hungarians“ already had certain words for cereals and for tools before their arrival in the Carpathian Basin, the author concludes that they were farmers. Yet elsewhere he writes that they obtained agricultural produce by raiding, or as tribute, that is to say as protection money.

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: Ibn Rusta writes that the chieftain of the Magyars rides at the head of 20,000 horsemen. This information is repeated more or less word for word by the other Muslim historians. How far that figure corresponds to the reality of the time cannot be determined precisely, but the truth will probably be far more conservative. Another matter is what we imagine by the term horseman: an elite heavy cavalryman in lamellar armour with an inlaid sabre and a luxurious composite bow, or a herdsman who, having no armour and no helmet, took with him to war his lasso, a bow, an axe and two simple spears. Even if we were to assume the figure of 20,000, then in such an army the „herdsmen“ would markedly outnumber the armoured horsemen. Although I use the word herdsman, thanks to the nomadic way of life he was a warrior trained all his life. A master in the use of the lasso for catching animals and an excellent archer, who, when he was not stealing other people’s animals, was defending his own herd against thieves. The famous Genghis Khan, too, began as a thief. From the archaeological finds in the Carpathian Basin it is evident that the Magyars had no heavy cavalry at all; only the commanders and the rulers’ personal guard had luxurious ornaments for dress and horse harness, and luxurious weapons.

Two rulers are already mentioned in the records of Ibn Rusta. In the first place under the word written in Arabic as k.nd.h., which is a rendering of the Magyar word kündä or kändä. Its form later changed, already in the Kingdom of Hungary, to kende. The Magyars took this title over from the Khazars, and it is used to denote the „supreme commander“. The second name could be written in today’s Hungarian as gyula. It is an open question whether the title belonged to a king who was at the same time also a spiritual leader, or only to a spiritual leader who performed some other function as well, for example that of judge. The brief records themselves do not allow the division of power and of the rulers’ tasks to be determined precisely. In any case, the Magyars had some form of dual rule.
The Magyars, Avars, Bulgars, Khazars, Pechenegs and Byzantines

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: István Zimonyi deals at length with the history of the nomads not only in the regions north of the Black Sea, but also with their penetration into the Balkans and into the Carpathian Basin. Drawing above all on the history of the Avars and the Bulgars, he presents not only the historic encounter of the nomads with the Slavs and the other inhabitants of the Carpathian Basin and the Balkans, but also their interactions with Christianity.
The Magyars, the Rus and the Slavs

The Muslim sources write that the Magyars are in a permanent state of war with the Rus and the Slavs and almost always win their battles. From the territories inhabited by the Rus and the Slavs they carry off captives, whom they sell to the Byzantines as slaves. This state of affairs corresponds to the reality before 850. Besides booty in the form of slaves, foodstuffs or livestock, raiding was also used to enforce the payment of tribute. The raids were mostly undertaken in winter, and this is why the Slavs, too, withdrew into their fortified strongholds, which we are accustomed to call hillforts. Until a society of farmers created an effective state power with professional warriors, it was practically defenceless against raids. After 850 the Norsemen (Vikings) began to create principalities in the territories of the Eastern Slavs. First in the north (Novgorod) and later also on the middle course of the river Dnieper. Within a few decades they had „levelled the score“, and the Slavicised rulers of Kyiv were attacking the nomads north of the Black Sea and in the Volga region. Later, however, the tables turned several times, and the raids of the nomads north of the Black Sea came to an end only in the time of the Empress Catherine the Great.

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: The Scandinavians had been trading with the Eastern Slavs ever since the year 500. In the course of the years 750 to 860 they built up centres along the trade routes leading from the Baltic all the way to the Black or the Caspian Sea. On the route to Constantinople, on the banks of the river Dnieper, Kyiv arose. In the chapter Kyiv and the Magyars, István Zimonyi deals with the situation just before the „Old Hungarians“ were driven out of the steppe and with their contacts with the Slavs in the Kyiv region. He offers three scenarios. The „Old Hungarians“ ruled in Kyiv and were driven out of it by the Rus; secondly, the „Old Hungarians“ administered Kyiv with the permission of the Khazar khans; or thirdly, they lived in relative peace with the Slavs and the Rus and took part in trade. Unfortunately, the author relies mainly on the Gesta Hungarorum, the Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum and the Nestor Chronicle, which are not exactly „bulletproof“ sources. But either way, it does allow one to form the idea that the leaders of the „Old Hungarians“ had, shortly before the „conquest of the homeland“, experience of ruling over Slavs and perhaps alongside Slavs.
The Magyars and the Slavs in the Carpathian Basin.

It was precisely the experience the „Old Hungarians“ gained with the Slavs and the Rus during their life north of the Black Sea that gave them an advantage in taking control of the Carpathian Basin. Although the author does not deal with the events after 895, in the book he addresses the question of the so-called double conquest of the homeland. He has clear reservations about the view that the Onogurs, who came to the Carpathian Basin in 670, were Magyars. As is traditional with Hungarian authors, Zimonyi also devotes attention to the geographical location of Great Moravia. Naturally, he mentions both „Great Moravias“ – „ours“, the northern one above the Danube, and the southern one in present-day Serbia. He lists the historical records, recalls the rich archaeological finds on the „Moravian Morava“ and the absence of any finds on the „Serbian“ Morava, and does not forget to mention the works of Hungarian authors either, but in the end he quite brilliantly avoids taking a clear position.

blocks.alt: Muslim sources on the Magyars before the Hungarian conquest

children.text: When we realise that the direct information concerning the „Old Hungarians“ would not fill even a single A4 page, while the book itself runs to 375 pages of the author’s own text, it is clear why, besides the „Old Hungarians“, we also learn a great deal about the Avars, the Burtas, the Khazars, the Onogurs, the Bulgars on the Volga and in the Balkans, and the other nomadic peoples of the time. It also provides a great deal of information about the Arabs, the Byzantines, the Persians and the Chinese, who were sometimes at peace with the nomads but more often at war. István Zimonyi uses written and archaeological sources from Herodotus to the medieval travellers to the Mongol capital. He does not single the „Old Hungarians“ out of the historical process as an exceptional people with extraordinary abilities; quite the contrary, by drawing on insights into the life, warfare and politics of the nomadic peoples from the northern frontiers of China to Pannonia, he deepens our insights into the Magyar people before their invasion of the Carpathian Basin. Understanding who the „Old Hungarians“ were before their invasion of the Carpathian Basin explains their success in the conquest of the homeland, and also the particular way in which they were transformed in the civilisationally and economically different environment of Central Europe.

The first and probably the best source is the work „Kitāb al-masālik wa-l-mamālik“ by the Persian vizier and geographer Abū ʿAbdallāh Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Jayhānī. Al-Jayhānī lived in the 10th century at the court of the Persian rulers and, thanks to his upbringing, his education and his position, he had access to older information and to diplomatic correspondence. His work „Kitāb al-masālik wa-l-mamālik“, in our language „The Book of Routes and Kingdoms“, has not survived in its original wording, but several copies exist. Besides the „Book of Routes and Kingdoms“, István Zimonyi uses above all the records of the following Muslim authors:

Although in terms of nationality they are a mixture of Arabs, Persians, Jews and scholars from Central Asia and from the Islamic regions of Spain, many of the authors listed take over information from their predecessors with greater or lesser accuracy. The author supplements the Muslim sources with information from western medieval chronicles and from Syriac, Armenian and Chinese sources, and very often draws on Byzantine sources as well, because the territories of the South Russian steppes were an area of power interest for the rulers in Constantinople.
